strings.name: Lu Xun
strings.role: Writer · A pioneer of modern literature
strings.summary: Lu Xun, born Zhou Shuren, was an important pioneer of modern Chinese literature. Stories such as A Madman’s Diary and The True Story of Ah Q examined society and the human condition. Essays, translations, work on ancient texts and literary history also broadened his contribution to new literature. He taught at several universities, wrote in Shanghai in his later years and supported young writers and the New Woodcut Movement. His work continues to influence Chinese writing and public debate.
strings.coverageNote: Selected, verifiable life events and works. Dates follow the cited institutions; this is not a day-by-day chronology.
strings.facts.fact-01.label: Birthplace
strings.facts.fact-02.label: Education
strings.facts.fact-02.value: School of Mines and Railways in Nanjing; left Sendai Medical School without graduating
strings.facts.fact-03.label: Notable works
strings.facts.fact-03.value: Call to Arms, Wandering, Wild Grass, A Brief History of Chinese Fiction
strings.highlights.highlight-01.title: Modern fiction
strings.highlights.highlight-01.text: Helped establish new literature through vernacular fiction and vividly drawn characters.
strings.highlights.highlight-02.title: Literary history and cultural work
strings.highlights.highlight-02.text: Wrote A Brief History of Chinese Fiction while also translating, editing and promoting woodcuts.
strings.timeline.event-01.title: Dies in Shanghai
strings.timeline.event-01.text: Continued writing, translating and editing in his later years; his writings were subsequently collected in the Complete Works of Lu Xun.
strings.timeline.event-02.title: Supports the New Woodcut Movement
strings.timeline.event-02.text: Organized woodcut teaching activities in Shanghai, served as an interpreter himself and supported young artists.
strings.timeline.event-03.title: Participates in the League of Left-Wing Writers
strings.timeline.event-03.text: Took part in the founding of the Chinese League of Left-Wing Writers and continued addressing social and cultural questions in essays.
strings.timeline.event-04.title: Moves to Shanghai
strings.timeline.event-04.text: Worked at Sun Yat-sen University before resigning and moving to Shanghai in October. Wild Grass was published that year.
strings.timeline.event-05.title: Publishes Wandering
strings.timeline.event-05.text: Left Beijing to teach at Xiamen University; his story collection Wandering appeared that year.
strings.timeline.event-06.title: Publishes Call to Arms
strings.timeline.event-06.text: His first collection of fiction appeared; the first volume of A Brief History of Chinese Fiction was also published that year.
strings.timeline.event-07.title: Begins publishing The True Story of Ah Q
strings.timeline.event-07.text: Used the character Ah Q to develop a critique of society in what became one of his most influential works of fiction.
strings.timeline.event-08.title: Publishes A Madman’s Diary
strings.timeline.event-08.text: First used the pen name Lu Xun for a vernacular story in New Youth, participating in the New Culture Movement.
strings.timeline.event-09.title: Turns from medicine to literature
strings.timeline.event-09.text: Discontinued medical studies in Japan and turned to literature, hoping to address social problems through writing.
strings.timeline.event-10.title: Goes to Japan to study
strings.timeline.event-10.text: Initially attended the Kobun Institute in Tokyo before entering Sendai Medical School in 1904.
strings.timeline.event-11.title: Born in Shaoxing
strings.timeline.event-11.text: Grew up in Shaoxing, Zhejiang, then attended modern schools in Nanjing, encountering natural science and translated works.
